summary: Provides terminology for benchmarking LAN switching devices. It extends the terminology of RFC 1242 and RFC 1944 to switches. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines shared terms for describing tests of LAN switches. The terms help readers understand what traffic a test used and what the switch did with it.

questions: how to benchmark a network switch
how do you measure switch performance
subtitle: A shared vocabulary for measuring how LAN switches handle frames and load.

tldr.problem: Switch benchmark results are hard to compare unless testers use the same terms for traffic patterns, load, and forwarding performance.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines terms for test setups, offered traffic, forwarding rates, congestion behavior, address handling, frame filtering, and broadcasts.
tldr.outcome: It extends earlier benchmarking terminology to LAN switching devices and provides definitions rather than a test procedure.

today: RFC 2285 is an Informational RFC published in February 1998. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Terminology Covers
sections.content:
The RFC extends existing benchmarking definitions to devices that switch frames at the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer. It defines language for test traffic, forwarding performance, congestion control, latency, address handling, and filtering.

It is a terminology document, not a test method. The RFC says readers should also consult RFC 1242 for general benchmarking terms and RFC 1944 for benchmarking methodology.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is a dictionary for switch tests. It names the kinds of traffic and measurements that a report should describe.

sections.title: Traffic Patterns and Load
sections.content:
Traffic orientation describes whether frames travel in one direction or whether every receiving interface also transmits. Traffic distribution describes how input interfaces map to output interfaces: one-to-one, many-to-one, one-to-many, or fully meshed.

The RFC also distinguishes intended load, which a test source tries to send, from offered load, which it is observed to send. Collisions or congestion control can make the offered load lower. A benchmark report must state offered load so readers can interpret its forwarding-rate result.
sections.plainLanguage: A test report needs to say which interfaces sent frames and which received them. It must also distinguish the traffic the test tried to send from the traffic that actually reached the switch.

sections.title: Forwarding and Other Measurements
sections.content:
Forwarding rate is the number of frames per second that a device successfully sends to the correct destination for a specified offered load. Maximum forwarding rate is the highest result in a set of measurements. Forwarding rate at maximum offered load is the result specifically at the test source’s maximum offered load, and that load must be reported.

Other definitions cover backpressure, forward pressure, head-of-line blocking, MAC address capacity and learning rate, flooded frames, errored frames, and broadcast forwarding rate and latency. These terms separate a switch’s behavior under different conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: A forwarding-rate number is meaningful only with its test load. Other measurements describe whether congestion slows unrelated traffic, how quickly addresses are learned, and how broadcasts or damaged frames are handled.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says benchmarking terminology does not directly affect network security when testing is not performed on devices or systems connected to operating networks. It notes that some switches may transmit frames more aggressively than link standards allow.

Such behavior does not itself create a security breach, but it can interfere with other devices’ access to the medium. The RFC discourages using those behaviors on the Internet or corporate networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The definitions themselves do not affect security. Testing or switch behavior can disrupt other devices if it takes place on a live network.
